clue.text: Where novel needs plot, political novel needs this?

definitions.text: Where novel needs plot, political novel needs this?

parts.words: Where novel needs plot, political novel needs this?
parts.note: a novel needs a plot, and a political novel needs a plot in the other sense: a secret scheme against the state

explanation.surface: A tip on the craft of fiction: every novel needs a storyline, and the political novel needs something extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' has two senses: the story of a novel and a secret scheme. The political thriller swaps the first sense for the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot in the sense of a secret scheme by several people against authority is a synonym.

clue.text: Old king of political economy?

definitions.meaning: the merry old king of the nursery rhyme who called for his pipe and bowl
G. D. H. ..., the English socialist writer on political economy

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme king and the 20th-century Oxford economist G. D. H. Cole share the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are names: the nursery-rhyme monarch and the Oxford socialist theorist share it.

clue.text: Nobody can identify submarine skipper

definitions.meaning: the Latin word for no one
the captain of the Nautilus in Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

explanation.walkthrough: Verne chose the Latin word for 'no one' as his captain's name, so the two senses are one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin pronoun meaning no one is also the name of Verne's undersea captain.

clue.text: Possibly no marital hop would be complete without it?

definitions.text: Possibly no marital hop would be complete without it?

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the following words may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A wry remark that a wedding dance would hardly be finished without something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges NO MARITAL HOP; the whole clue then describes the result, a song celebrating a coming marriage (Spenser wrote one), which a wedding would be incomplete without.
explanation.definitionFit: A song written in celebration of a forthcoming wedding is what a marriage festivity calls for.

clue.text: Poe's bells kept time in this sort of rhyme

definitions.text: Poe's bells kept time in this sort of rhyme

parts.words: Poe's bells kept time in this sort of rhyme
parts.note: a quotation from Poe's poem The Bells: 'Keeping time, time, time, / In a sort of ... rhyme'

explanation.surface: A reminder of the rhythm of Poe's famous bell poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer completes the line from Poe's The Bells, where the sleigh bells keep time 'in a sort of' ancient Norse-lettered rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the ancient Germanic alphabet of carved letters, which Poe used for a mysterious, incantatory rhyme.

clue.text: Eponymous features by Compton Mackenzie and Edith Wharton amount to miles of dead creatures in Australia

definitions.text: miles of dead creatures in Australia

parts.note: Coral is a 1925 novel by Compton Mackenzie, named after its title character
The Reef is a 1912 novel by Edith Wharton

explanation.surface: Two novel titles add up to a natural wonder off the coast of Queensland.
explanation.walkthrough: Each author supplies the title of one of their novels: Mackenzie's Coral and Wharton's The Reef. Together they name the Great Barrier formation, which is built from the skeletons of tiny sea creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: A long ridge built from the skeletons of tiny marine polyps, like the Great Barrier one off Queensland.

clue.text: "As it-, it ain't. That's logic" (Lewis Carroll)

definitions.text: "As it-, it ain't. That's logic" (Lewis Carroll)

parts.words: "As it-, it ain't. That's logic" (Lewis Carroll)
parts.note: Tweedledee's speech in Through the Looking-Glass with one word blanked out, which the solver fills in

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap, from Tweedledee's mock-logical speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledee says: 'if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it ---, it ain't. That's logic.' The missing word is the contraction of 'is not'.
explanation.definitionFit: The contraction of 'is not' fills the gap, matching the colloquial 'ain't' that follows it.

clue.text: It "is an Impressionist painting", said Trevor. "It should be an explosion of truth"

definitions.text: It "is an Impressionist painting", said Trevor. "It should be an explosion of truth"

parts.words: It "is an Impressionist painting", said Trevor. "It should be an explosion of truth"
parts.note: William Trevor, the Irish writer, describing the brief prose form in which he was a master

explanation.surface: A writer's famous description of his own art form.
explanation.walkthrough: William Trevor was celebrated for brief fiction; he called the form 'an Impressionist painting, a glimpse... an explosion of truth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trevor's description fits a brief prose fiction, a glimpse rather than a full novel-length narrative.

clue.text: Ronald Harwood's kitchen piece?

definitions.meaning: Harwood's 1980 play about an actor-manager and his wardrobe assistant
a sideboard with shelves for crockery, a piece of kitchen furniture

explanation.walkthrough: Harwood's play is named after the backstage assistant who helps an actor into costume; the same word is a kitchen cupboard with shelves.
explanation.definitionFit: Harwood's play title is also the name of a shelved cupboard for plates found in kitchens.

clue.text: Oral eponym, perhaps, suggesting personal satire

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters of the words before it could form something else

explanation.surface: A pun about the man whose name became a word for slips of the tongue, as a kind of satire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oral eponym' points at Spooner, whose spoken slips gave us a word, but 'perhaps' simply rearranges ORAL EPONYM.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocking ridicule of an individual in writing is satire aimed at a person.

clue.text: Money for old Hamilton work easily earned?

definitions.text: Money for old Hamilton work easily earned?

parts.words: Money for old Hamilton work easily earned?
parts.note: the idiom 'money for old ---' means pay for easy work, and Patrick Hamilton wrote a play of that one-word title

explanation.surface: A remark about easily earned cash, dropping the name of a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money for old rope' is a British idiom for pay for very little work. Patrick Hamilton wrote the 1929 play Rope, later filmed by Hitchcock.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for an easy wage ends with this word for cord, also the title of Hamilton's thriller play.

clue.text: Waugh protagonist offering small change with a light touch

parts.note: a penny is a small coin
a feather gives a very light touch

explanation.surface: Evelyn Waugh's hero dispensing a little money gently.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Pennyfeather is the hapless hero of Evelyn Waugh's first novel, Decline and Fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul is the naive central character of Waugh's Decline and Fall, so this surname names the lead.

clue.text: The colonel, reader of Fowles book

parts.note: Col is the usual abbreviation for the military rank colonel
a lector is a reader, in a church service or a university

explanation.surface: A list of characters: an army officer and someone who reads, in a Fowles novel.
explanation.walkthrough: John Fowles's first novel is about a man who kidnaps a woman as if adding her to his butterfly set.
explanation.definitionFit: John Fowles's 1963 debut novel takes its title from its butterfly-obsessed kidnapper.

clue.text: Elegant sin wrongly identified with Shelley's lush roses

indicators.note: wrongly signals that the letters of the phrase are set out in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Moral disapproval of an elegant sin, linked to Shelley's flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongly' looks like moral comment on the sin but rearranges ELEGANT SIN. Sweetbriar roses appear in Romantic verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetbriar, a wild rose, appears in Shelley's poems as a lush climbing flower.

clue.text: One more competent expires outside, due to knavish tricks

indicators.note: outside means the word for expires is placed round the other pieces

parts.note: to expire is to die, so expires gives dies
one is the Roman numeral I
abler means more able, more competent

explanation.surface: Someone more capable dies, and something follows from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' wraps the word for expires round the other two pieces, splitting it after its first letter. A diablerie is literally devil's work, from French diable.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word means devilry: mischievous, wicked tricks.

clue.text: Lake surrounded by cunning wavy ornamental border

indicators.note: surrounded by means the word for lake sits inside the word for cunning

parts.note: guile means cunning or craftiness
loch is the Scottish word for a lake

explanation.surface: A lake ringed by a crafty, wavy decorative edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surrounded by' sets the Scottish lake inside the word for cunning, just before its final letter. A guilloche is the twisted-band pattern seen on banknotes.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative pattern of interlaced curving lines, used on banknotes and architecture, forming a border.

clue.text: Keyboard instrument comes with fashionable interior for Bentley domestic

indicators.note: interior means the word for fashionable goes inside the instrument

parts.note: a celeste, or celesta, is a keyboard instrument with steel plates struck by hammers
in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'

explanation.surface: A keyboard instrument with a stylish inside, belonging to a Bentley servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interior' sets the word for fashionable inside the instrument, just before its final letter. The celeste is the bell-like keyboard heard in Tchaikovsky's Sugar Plum Fairy dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Celestine is the name of a maid, a household servant in Bentley's writing.

clue.text: Dostoevsky's jottings on the Tube?

parts.note: Dostoevsky's ... from Underground, with the London Tube standing in for 'underground'

explanation.surface: A great Russian novelist scribbling on the London metro.
explanation.walkthrough: The London Tube is the Underground, so jottings 'from Underground' become Dostoevsky's 1864 novella.
explanation.definitionFit: Jottings are brief written records, and Dostoevsky's novella title opens with this word.

clue.text: Repository for Elia's poems

parts.note: Elia was the pen name of Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A place where an essayist's poems are kept.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb wrote as 'Elia'; his 1830 Album Verses were poems written for friends' keepsake books.
explanation.definitionFit: A blank book for keeping verses, autographs or pictures is a repository of that kind.

clue.text: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw

definitions.text: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw

parts.words: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw
parts.note: echoes 'may the force be with you', addressed to the hero of Shaw's Man and Superman, which centres on a vital creative energy

explanation.surface: Shaw wishing his hero well, in the words of a later film blessing.
explanation.walkthrough: John Tanner is the hero of Man and Superman, in which Shaw expounds the vital, evolutionary energy driving humanity.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's term for the creative evolutionary energy driving living things, central to his philosophy.

clue.text: Let slip by Forsyth

parts.note: Mark Antony's 'Cry havoc and let slip the ...' in Julius Caesar, and the title of a Frederick Forsyth novel

explanation.surface: Something a novelist accidentally revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let slip' sounds like an accidental disclosure but completes Shakespeare's line, 'Cry havoc, and let slip...', which Frederick Forsyth took for his mercenary novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's phrase for the hounds of battle unleashed became the title of Forsyth's mercenary thriller.

clue.text: Clown is second in gala

indicators.note: in places the letter for second inside the word for gala

parts.note: a fete is a gala, an outdoor festive event

explanation.surface: A clown is the second act at a gala.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste is the clown in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night. 'In' puts S inside FETE.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste is the jester, the professional fool, in Twelfth Night.

clue.text: Norse peer

parts.note: Peer is the first name of Ibsen's Norwegian hero, so this asks for his surname

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a lord but is the first name of Ibsen's Norwegian hero, whose surname is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Ibsen's restless Norwegian hero, whose first name is the clue's last word.

clue.text: William Morris's lacked provenance

parts.note: Morris's utopian romance is ... from Nowhere, and something from nowhere has no known source

explanation.surface: A complaint that a Morris piece had no recorded origin.
explanation.walkthrough: Something that lacks provenance comes 'from nowhere', which completes William Morris's 1890 title News from Nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidings or reports, the first word of Morris's utopian title, here coming from nowhere.

clue.text: Primitive from China, I fancy

indicators.note: from signals that the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A piece of primitive art from China, as I imagine it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across 'chiNA I Fancy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A naive, untrained artist or artwork is primitive in style.

clue.text: She's my nice new heroine, subject to Grant

indicators.note: new signals that the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as its letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone proudly introduces their latest heroine, the subject of a grant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like a gift of money but is James Grant, the Scottish novelist; 'new' rearranges SHE'S MY NICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Cheyne is the title heroine of James Grant's 1883 novel, the subject of his story.

clue.text: American in 7 is hero of 1925 German novel

indicators.note: in means the American letters go inside the abbreviation

parts.note: 7-down is short story, abbreviated SS

explanation.surface: An American in a story turns out to be a German novel's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 7 is 7-down, whose two words are shortened to their initials; 'in' places the American abbreviation within. Jud Süss is Lion Feuchtwanger's 1925 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Süss Oppenheimer is the title figure of Feuchtwanger's 1925 novel Jew Süss.

clue.text: Pompey supporter gives 'em net scare, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that these letters might be reordered

parts.note: short for them, taken as its letters

explanation.surface: A soldier's ally frightens them with a net.
explanation.walkthrough: Menecrates is one of Pompey's followers in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra; 'perhaps' rearranges EM NET SCARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Menecrates appears as a follower of Sextus Pompeius in Antony and Cleopatra, a supporter in his cause.
